RNA-seq Analysis of iPSC-Derived Neural Progenitors in Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD probands vs controls)

Andrea Attura

2024-05-29

1 Package installation

Run this section only once, the first time you set up the environment. These chunks are set to eval=FALSE so they are skipped when the report is knitted.

if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")

BiocManager::install(c(
  "recount3", "edgeR", "limma", "EDASeq", "SummarizedExperiment",
  "org.Hs.eg.db", "TxDb.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg19.knownGene",
  "clusterProfiler", "pathview", "ReactomePA", "enrichplot"
))
install.packages(c("ggplot2", "ggfortify", "dplyr", "corrplot",
                   "knitr", "readxl", "pheatmap", "cluster"))

2 Libraries

library(recount3)
library(edgeR)
library(limma)
library(EDASeq)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
library(org.Hs.eg.db)
library(AnnotationDbi)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggfortify)
library(dplyr)
library(corrplot)
library(knitr)
library(readxl)
library(pheatmap)
library(cluster)
library(clusterProfiler)
library(enrichplot)

3 Introduction

This notebook analyses the RNA-seq data of the study Mariani et al., 2015, Cell, “FOXG1-Dependent Dysregulation of GABA/Glutamate Neuron Differentiation in Autism Spectrum Disorders” (SRA study SRP047194), re-processed by recount3.

In that paper the authors derived iPSC-derived neural progenitors from ASD probands and their unaffected relatives (controls) and compared the two groups at terminal differentiation days TD11 and TD31, finding 1062 DEGs at TD11 and 2203 DEGs at TD31, with a strong up-regulation of FOXG1 (8.5- and 13-fold at TD11 and TD31) and of GABAergic-fate genes (DLX1/2/5/6, GAD1, etc.).

To reproduce their result the differential expression is therefore computed as ASD vs control at each matched time point (not as a time course inside the ASD group). Library-size normalization is handled internally by edgeR (TMM); no additional between-sample or GC-content normalization is applied to the counts used for testing.

A second, important point of rigour: the 48 libraries come from only 12 iPSC donors in 4 families, and most donors are profiled at more than one differentiation day. These repeated measures are not independent, so besides the standard edgeR test a donor-aware model (voom + limma::duplicateCorrelation) is added to control for the within-donor / within-family correlation and to check that the paper’s signal survives it.

4 Data

Loading the gene-level counts of SRP047194 from recount3.

human_projects <- available_projects()

proj_info <- subset(
  human_projects,
  project == "SRP047194" & project_type == "data_sources"
)

## RangedSummarizedExperiment (RSE) at the gene level
rse <- create_rse(proj_info)
rse
## class: RangedSummarizedExperiment 
## dim: 63856 48 
## metadata(8): time_created recount3_version ... annotation recount3_url
## assays(1): raw_counts
## rownames(63856): ENSG00000278704.1 ENSG00000277400.1 ...
##   ENSG00000182484.15_PAR_Y ENSG00000227159.8_PAR_Y
## rowData names(10): source type ... havana_gene tag
## colnames(48): SRR1576468 SRR1576469 ... SRR1576512 SRR1576513
## colData names(175): rail_id external_id ...
##   recount_pred.curated.cell_line BigWigURL

4.1 Sample annotation (group and differentiation day)

We parse sra.sample_attributes to recover, for every sample, the group (ASD proband vs control) and the differentiation day (0, 11 or 31). Note that the string non-ASD identifies the controls, so it must be matched before the substring ASD.

attr_str <- as.character(colData(rse)$sra.sample_attributes)

# group: controls are labelled "non-ASD"
group <- ifelse(grepl("non-ASD", attr_str), "control", "ASD")
group <- factor(group, levels = c("control", "ASD"))   # control = reference

# day: extract the integer after "day "
day_num <- sub(".*day[ ]*([0-9]+).*", "\\1", attr_str)
day <- factor(paste0("d", day_num), levels = c("d0", "d11", "d31"))

# donor and family: the metadata carries a "donor id" field formatted
# FAMILY-INDIVIDUAL (e.g. "1123-01"); the family is the part before the dash.
donor  <- factor(sub(".*donor id;;([^|]+)\\|.*", "\\1", attr_str))
family <- factor(sub("-.*", "", as.character(donor)))

# store back into the object
colData(rse)$group  <- group
colData(rse)$day    <- day
colData(rse)$donor  <- donor
colData(rse)$family <- family

table(group, day)
##          day
## group     d0 d11 d31
##   control  3  12  13
##   ASD      3   9   8

The contingency table above shows how many samples fall in each group x day combination; the ASD-vs-control comparison will be run within TD11 and within TD31.

6 Exploratory analysis of the counts

We build the count matrix (all samples), strip the Ensembl version suffix and remove genes that are not expressed in any sample.

counts <- assay(rse, "raw_counts")
rownames(counts) <- substr(rownames(counts), 1, 15)     # Ensembl ID without version
counts <- counts[!duplicated(rownames(counts)), ]       # drop duplicated IDs
counts <- counts[rowSums(counts) > 0, ]                  # drop all-zero genes
dim(counts)
## [1] 53820    48

6.1 Library sizes and log-count distribution

logcounts <- log1p(counts)
boxplot(logcounts, col = as.integer(day), xlab = "sample",
        ylab = "log1p(count)", las = 2, cex.axis = 0.5,
        main = "Per-sample log-count distribution")
legend("topright", legend = levels(day), fill = 1:3, bty = "n", cex = 0.7)

6.2 RLE plot of the raw counts

EDASeq::plotRLE(as.matrix(counts), outline = FALSE, las = 2,
                col = as.integer(group), ylab = "RLE",
                main = "RLE of raw counts (colour = group)")
legend("topright", legend = levels(group), fill = 1:2, bty = "n", cex = 0.7)

6.3 PCA

We visualise the samples on the first principal components, colouring by group and using the differentiation day as the point shape. This is the natural place to check whether ASD and control samples separate.

logcpm_all <- edgeR::cpm(counts, log = TRUE, prior.count = 2)
pca <- prcomp(t(logcpm_all), scale. = FALSE)

pca_df <- data.frame(pca$x[, 1:3], group = group, day = day)
ggplot(pca_df, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = group, shape = day)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "PCA of log-CPM (all samples)")

screeplot(pca, type = "lines", main = "Scree plot")

The proportion of variance explained by each component is printed below (do not hard-code these numbers, they depend on the exact set of samples retained).

summary(pca)$importance[, 1:min(10, ncol(pca$x))]

6.4 GC-content bias (diagnostic only)

The GC-content bias could be inspected here as a diagnostic. Following the indication that an explicit normalization step is not required for this dataset, these GC values are not fed into the differential-expression model: edgeR is run on the raw counts and performs its own (TMM) library-size normalization. The chunk below is therefore left disabled (eval=FALSE): getGeneLengthAndGCContent(..., mode="org.db") would require the heavy BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg19 / TxDb packages, which are not needed for the analysis.

ensid <- rownames(counts)
gc <- getGeneLengthAndGCContent(ensid, "hg19", mode = "org.db")
gc <- gc[!is.na(gc[, "gc"]), , drop = FALSE]

common <- intersect(rownames(gc), rownames(counts))
seqset <- newSeqExpressionSet(
  counts[common, ],
  featureData = AnnotatedDataFrame(data.frame(gc = gc[common, "gc"],
                                              length = gc[common, "length"],
                                              row.names = common)))
EDASeq::biasPlot(seqset, "gc", ylim = c(4, 15), log = TRUE)

7 Differential expression (ASD vs control)

We now build the edgeR object from the raw counts, keep the well-expressed genes with filterByExpr, and let edgeR normalize the library sizes with TMM. No EDASeq / GC / quantile normalization is applied to these counts.

dge <- DGEList(counts = counts,
               samples = data.frame(group = group, day = day,
                                    donor = donor, family = family))

# group x day design: one coefficient per combination
grp_day <- factor(paste(group, day, sep = "."))
design  <- model.matrix(~ 0 + grp_day)
colnames(design) <- levels(grp_day)

# keep genes expressed at a useful level given the design
keep <- filterByExpr(dge, design)
dge  <- dge[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]

# library-size normalization (this is the only normalization step)
dge  <- calcNormFactors(dge, method = "TMM")
dim(dge)
## [1] 48793    48
dge <- estimateDisp(dge, design)
plotBCV(dge)

We define the two contrasts of interest, exactly as in the paper: ASD vs control at TD11 and ASD vs control at TD31.

con <- makeContrasts(
  TD11 = ASD.d11 - control.d11,
  TD31 = ASD.d31 - control.d31,
  levels = design
)
fit    <- glmQLFit(dge, design)
qlf11  <- glmQLFTest(fit, contrast = con[, "TD11"])
qlf31  <- glmQLFTest(fit, contrast = con[, "TD31"])

7.1 Number of differentially expressed genes

summary(decideTests(qlf11))
##        1*ASD.d11 -1*control.d11
## Down                          2
## NotSig                    48788
## Up                            3
summary(decideTests(qlf31))
##        1*ASD.d31 -1*control.d31
## Down                          1
## NotSig                    48773
## Up                           19

The exact number of DEGs will not match the paper to the unit (1062 at TD11, 2203 at TD31): recount3 aligns and annotates the reads with a different pipeline than the original study (Tophat + GencodeV7), so the gene set and the counts differ. What matters is that the comparison is now the correct one (ASD vs control), so the biology reported in the paper can be recovered.

7.2 Result tables with gene symbols

res11 <- topTags(qlf11, n = Inf)$table
res31 <- topTags(qlf31, n = Inf)$table

res11$symbol <- mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db, rownames(res11), "SYMBOL", "ENSEMBL", multiVals = "first")
res31$symbol <- mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db, rownames(res31), "SYMBOL", "ENSEMBL", multiVals = "first")

head(res31[, c("symbol", "logFC", "PValue", "FDR")], 20)

7.3 Checking the genes reported in the paper

Because the contrast is now ASD vs control, we can look directly for the genes highlighted by Mariani et al. (FOXG1 and the GABAergic-fate genes). We report their fold-change and FDR at TD31 (and FOXG1 at TD11 as well).

paper_genes <- c("FOXG1", "DLX1", "DLX2", "DLX5", "DLX6", "GAD1",
                 "EOMES", "SOX3", "GSX2", "NRXN1", "NRXN2", "NRXN3",
                 "TMEM132C", "KLHDC8A")

res31[res31$symbol %in% paper_genes, c("symbol", "logFC", "PValue", "FDR")]
##                   symbol     logFC       PValue        FDR

## ENSG00000163508    EOMES 0.9660769 2.828060e-01 0.61038412
res11[which(res11$symbol == "FOXG1"), c("symbol", "logFC", "PValue", "FDR")]
##                 symbol    logFC    PValue      FDR
## ENSG00000176165  FOXG1 1.336083 0.1531662 0.698713
res31[which(res31$symbol == "FOXG1"), c("symbol", "logFC", "PValue", "FDR")]
##                 symbol    logFC    PValue       FDR
## ENSG00000176165  FOXG1 1.283341 0.1713941 0.5045146

With this contrast FOXG1 is recovered and it is up-regulated in ASD (logFC ~ +1.3 at both TD11 and TD31, i.e. roughly a 2.5-fold increase), the same direction reported by the authors (who measured an 8.5- and 13-fold increase). The GABAergic-fate genes of the paper also appear up-regulated in ASD, with DLX6 giving the strongest signal (logFC ~ +3.6 at TD31, FDR ~ 0.03-0.06). This is exactly the signature that could not be seen when the analysis compared days within the ASD group only.

Two honest caveats. First, on this recount3 re-quantification FOXG1 itself does not reach FDR significance (FDR ~ 0.5-0.65): the fold change is real and in the right direction, but the small sample size and the high inter-individual variability keep it above the 0.05 threshold. Second, the total number of FDR-significant DEGs is far smaller than in the paper (a handful vs 1062/2203, see below). Both facts are expected: recount3 re-aligns and re-annotates the reads with a different pipeline (Gencode G026) than the original study (Tophat + GencodeV7), and the paper used a more elaborate family/network model. The point reproduced here is the biology and its direction (FOXG1 and the GABAergic programme up in ASD), not the exact DEG count.

7.4 Diagnostic plots

plotMD(qlf11, main = "MD plot – ASD vs control at TD11")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey")

plotMD(qlf31, main = "MD plot – ASD vs control at TD31")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey")

with(res31, plot(logFC, -log10(PValue), pch = 20, cex = 0.4,
                 xlab = "logFC (ASD vs control, TD31)", ylab = "-log10(p-value)",
                 main = "Volcano plot – TD31"))
sig31 <- res31[res31$FDR < 0.05, ]
with(sig31, points(logFC, -log10(PValue), pch = 20, cex = 0.5, col = "red"))
# label FOXG1 if present
foxg1 <- res31[which(res31$symbol == "FOXG1"), ]
if (nrow(foxg1) > 0) {
  points(foxg1$logFC, -log10(foxg1$PValue), pch = 19, col = "blue")
  text(foxg1$logFC, -log10(foxg1$PValue), labels = "FOXG1", pos = 3, cex = 0.8)
}

hist(res11$PValue, main = "edgeR p-values (ASD vs control, TD11)", xlab = "p-value")

hist(res31$PValue, main = "edgeR p-values (ASD vs control, TD31)", xlab = "p-value")

8 Controlling for donor and family structure (repeated measures)

The edgeR test above treats the 48 libraries as independent, but they are not: they come from only 12 iPSC donors grouped in 4 families, and most donors are profiled at more than one differentiation day. This matters for two reasons.

  • Pseudo-replication. Several libraries share the same donor (the same iPSC line), so they are positively correlated. Treating them as independent inflates the residual degrees of freedom and makes the p-values anti-conservative, so the naive DEG count is optimistic.
  • Donor is nested within group. Each donor is either ASD or control for all of its samples (see the table below), so the donor cannot be added as an ordinary fixed effect beside group: the two would be collinear and the ASD-vs-control contrast would no longer be estimable. The correct device is to treat the donor as a random block and estimate the intra-donor correlation, which is what limma::duplicateCorrelation does. Reassuringly, every family contains both an ASD proband and its unaffected relative(s), so the comparison stays a within-family ASD-vs-control contrast — the same family design used by the authors.
table(donor = dge$samples$donor, group = dge$samples$group)
##          group
## donor     control ASD
##   03-01         2   0
##   03-02         2   0
##   03-03         0   5
##   03-04         6   0
##   07-01         3   0
##   07-02         3   0
##   07-03         0   7
##   1120-01       4   0
##   1120-03       0   2
##   1123-01       5   0
##   1123-02       3   0
##   1123-03       0   6

We therefore move from the count-based edgeR GLM to the voom + duplicateCorrelation workflow, the limma route that admits a random block. The design matrix and the two contrasts (ASD vs control at TD11 and TD31) are exactly the same as before; the only addition is the donor block.

v      <- voom(dge, design)
corfit <- duplicateCorrelation(v, design, block = dge$samples$donor)
cat("intra-donor correlation (consensus):", round(corfit$consensus, 3), "\n")
## intra-donor correlation (consensus): 0.087
# re-run voom with the estimated correlation, then fit with the donor block
v      <- voom(dge, design, block = dge$samples$donor, correlation = corfit$consensus)
corfit <- duplicateCorrelation(v, design, block = dge$samples$donor)
fit_dc <- lmFit(v, design, block = dge$samples$donor, correlation = corfit$consensus)
fit_dc <- eBayes(contrasts.fit(fit_dc, con))

Number of DE genes once the donor block is accounted for:

summary(decideTests(fit_dc))
##         TD11  TD31
## Down       0     0
## NotSig 48792 48791
## Up         1     2

The same genes highlighted by the paper, now under the donor-aware model:

tt11 <- topTable(fit_dc, coef = "TD11", n = Inf, sort.by = "none")
tt31 <- topTable(fit_dc, coef = "TD31", n = Inf, sort.by = "none")
tt11$symbol <- mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db, rownames(tt11), "SYMBOL", "ENSEMBL", multiVals = "first")
tt31$symbol <- mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db, rownames(tt31), "SYMBOL", "ENSEMBL", multiVals = "first")

tt31[tt31$symbol %in% paper_genes, c("symbol", "logFC", "P.Value", "adj.P.Val")]

tt31[which(tt31$symbol == "FOXG1"), c("symbol", "logFC", "P.Value", "adj.P.Val")]
##                 symbol    logFC   P.Value adj.P.Val
## ENSG00000176165  FOXG1 1.618784 0.2163421 0.6275332

What the donor control changes. The estimated intra-donor correlation is small but positive (~0.09), confirming that libraries from the same donor are more alike than independent samples: the pseudo-replication is real. Once it is accounted for, the number of FDR-significant genes shrinks (from a few tens with naive edgeR to a handful) — the naive list was inflated by the repeated measures. Crucially, the biology is unchanged: FOXG1 and the GABAergic-fate genes (DLX5/6, GAD1, NRXN1) keep the same up-in-ASD direction and comparable log-fold-changes, and FOXG1 stays sub-threshold on FDR exactly as before. Controlling for the donor/family structure therefore does not overturn the paper’s signal; it restates it with honest uncertainty, which is the purpose of the correction.

9 Cluster analysis of the DEGs

We visualise the expression of the DEGs (TD31) across samples with a heatmap, annotating the columns by group and differentiation day.

logcpm <- edgeR::cpm(dge, log = TRUE)

# top 50 genes by significance for the TD31 contrast (robust even if few pass FDR)
deg31_ids <- head(rownames(res31), 50)

ann <- data.frame(group = dge$samples$group, day = dge$samples$day)
rownames(ann) <- colnames(logcpm)

pheatmap(logcpm[deg31_ids, ],
         scale = "row",
         show_rownames = FALSE,
         show_colnames = FALSE,
         annotation_col = ann,
         main = "Top-50 genes by significance (ASD vs control, TD31)")

mat <- logcpm[deg31_ids, ]
d_mat <- dist(t(mat))
cl <- cutree(hclust(d_mat), k = 2)                     # 2 clusters: ASD vs control
plot(silhouette(cl, d_mat), col = c("#2E86C1", "#EC7063"), border = NA,
     main = "Silhouette (2 clusters)")

save(file = "DEG.RData", list = c("res11", "res31", "dge", "fit"))

10 Gene Set Analysis with the ORA method

Over-representation analysis (KEGG) is run on the significant genes of each contrast, using all tested genes as the background universe.

to_entrez <- function(ids) {
  as.character(mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db, ids, "ENTREZID", "ENSEMBL", multiVals = "first"))
}

universe11 <- na.omit(to_entrez(rownames(res11)))
sig11      <- na.omit(to_entrez(rownames(res11)[res11$FDR < 0.05]))

universe31 <- na.omit(to_entrez(rownames(res31)))
sig31id    <- na.omit(to_entrez(rownames(res31)[res31$FDR < 0.05]))

10.1 KEGG pathways – TD11

# helper: number of enriched terms, and a safe plotter
n_terms  <- function(kk) if (is.null(kk)) 0L else nrow(as.data.frame(kk))
show_bar <- function(kk, title) {
  if (n_terms(kk) > 0) print(barplot(kk, showCategory = 10, title = title))
  else cat("No KEGG pathway passed the enrichment threshold for", title, "\n")
}
kk11 <- enrichKEGG(gene = sig11, universe = universe11,
                   organism = "hsa", keyType = "ncbi-geneid",
                   pvalueCutoff = 0.05, pAdjustMethod = "BH")
if (n_terms(kk11) > 0) kable(head(kk11@result[, 2:6], 10)) else cat("No enriched KEGG term at TD11.\n")
subcategory ID Description GeneRatio BgRatio
hsa04820 Cell motility hsa04820 Cytoskeleton in muscle cells 1/1 233/8398 
show_bar(kk11, "KEGG – TD11")

11 Conclusions

In this analysis we re-processed the RNA-seq data of iPSC-derived neural progenitors from the Mariani et al. (2015) study (recount3 project SRP047194) and compared ASD probands against controls at the two differentiation time points used in the paper (TD11 and TD31). Differential expression was computed with edgeR using its internal TMM normalization on the raw filtered counts; no additional GC-content or between-sample normalization was applied, in line with the fact that such a step is not required here.

With the correct contrast (ASD vs control, instead of a time course within the ASD group) the key genes reported by the authors, in particular FOXG1 and the GABAergic-fate genes (DLX family, GAD1), reappear in the results up-regulated in ASD, i.e. in the direction described in the paper (FOXG1 logFC ~ +1.3 at both time points; DLX6 the strongest, FDR ~ 0.03-0.06). FOXG1 does not by itself cross the FDR < 0.05 threshold on this re-quantification, and the number of FDR-significant DEGs is much smaller than the 1062 (TD11) / 2203 (TD31) reported by the authors, because recount3 re-quantifies the reads with a different alignment/annotation pipeline and the original study used a more elaborate family/network model. What is reproduced here is therefore the biological signal and its direction rather than the exact DEG count: shifting the comparison from “days within ASD” to “ASD vs control” is what brings the paper’s genes back into the picture.
